Ericsson\") Olympic gold and silver medalist in speed skating\\n\\nCulture\\n-------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=20 \"Edit section: Culture\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Ostra_Aradalen1_Sweden.jpg/250px-Ostra_Aradalen1_Sweden.jpg)](/wiki/File:Ostra_Aradalen1_Sweden.jpg)\\n\\nTraditional summer houses, *buvåll* \"critter house\" in Jämtland. \\'Bu\\' is [cognate](/wiki/Cognate \"Cognate\") to the English word \"booth\" and \\'våll\\' to \"[weald](/wiki/Weald \"Weald\")\"\\n\\n[![Goats at Gräftåvallen, southern Jämtland](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Gr%C3%A4ft%C3%A5vallen.jpg/250px-Gr%C3%A4ft%C3%A5vallen.jpg)](/wiki/File:Gr%C3%A4ft%C3%A5vallen.jpg \"Goats at Gräftåvallen, southern Jämtland\")\\n\\nGoats at Gräftåvallen, southern Jämtland\\n\\n[![Jämthund](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/J%C3%A4mthund_drvd.png/250px-J%C3%A4mthund_drvd.png)](/wiki/File:J%C3%A4mthund_drvd.png \"Jämthund\")\\n\\nJämthund\\n\\nThe culture of Jämtland has been greatly affected by the fact that Jämtland has never had an [upper class](/wiki/Upper_class \"Upper class\"), since the population have mostly consisted of free sovereign farmers with wide connections and a strong regional identity.[[26]](#cite_note-26) This has been the case for many generations. When [Christian IV of Denmark](/wiki/Christian_IV_of_Denmark \"Christian IV of Denmark\") punished the Jamts severely after having sworn the Swedish king their allegiance (see above) by turning them into [tenant farmers](/wiki/Tenant_farmer \"Tenant farmer\") and abolished their seal, he told them to stay put on their farms. They did not heed this call but instead sought help from their own organized advisors and \"the land\\'s defense\", an insolence that further outraged the Danish king. Jämtland started out free and remained autonomous during its time as a Norwegian [dependency](/wiki/Dependent_territory \"Dependent territory\"). Because of Jämtland\\'s historical background the local culture shows great similarities with the [Norwegian farm culture](/wiki/Norwegian_farm_culture \"Norwegian farm culture\").\\n\\nToday, the history of Jämtland is exhibited in the regional museum [Jamtli](/wiki/Jamtli \"Jamtli\") in [Östersund](/wiki/%C3%96stersund \"Östersund\"). The museum consists of an [open-air section](/wiki/Open-air_museum \"Open-air museum\") with historical buildings, as well as an indoor museum which houses exhibitions about the region\\'s cultural history, from the Stone Age until modern times. Local history has been very popular in Jämtland for over 100 years, due to the extensive cultural home ground movement that emerged in the late 19th and early 20th century. The movement founded Jamtli to preserve the cultural heritage.\\n\\n### Lifestyle\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=21 \"Edit section: Lifestyle\")]\\n\\nThe culture in Jämtland has been marked by the stages in human development; the hunting-gathering stage, the semi-nomadic herding stage, the fully agricultural stage and the modern technological stage.\\n\\nRemnants from the hunter-gathering stage is first and foremost hunting itself. Jämtland\\'s population remained in this stage for a very long time due to the hunters ability to sustain the population. Today the moose hunt is regarded by many Jamts as the major holiday of the year. When the first humans came to Jämtland they brought dogs with them as helpers. The local dog, [Jämthund](/wiki/J%C3%A4mthund \"Jämthund\"), is a canine breed eponymous to Jämtland. Even if it is not explicitly stated, popular perception holds that the dog depicted in the coat of arms is of that breed. The Jämthund is often described having a [wolf](/wiki/Wolf \"Wolf\")-like appearance.\\n\\nOne of the first things [Tacitus](/wiki/Tacitus \"Tacitus\") mentions in his work *[Germania](/wiki/Germania_(book) \"Germania (book)\")* is that the Germanic people treasure their animals above all else. Tacitus also concludes that the Germanic people found cultivation repulsive. Instead, he states, the Germanic people devote themselves to food and sleep and besides that they prefer to remain idle. All of this, to certain extents, applied to Jämtland. When the people of Jämtland settled down they relied mostly on [pastoralism](/wiki/Pastoralism \"Pastoralism\") ([transhumance](/wiki/Transhumance \"Transhumance\")). Their animals were the source of wealth and they were therefore loved by their owners. This love for the [livestock](/wiki/Livestock \"Livestock\") has manifested itself in the dialect, a male [nipple](/wiki/Nipple \"Nipple\") is called *bokkjen* (the [buck](/wiki/Goat#Etymology \"Goat\")) and a female nipple is known as *geita* (the [goat](/wiki/Goat \"Goat\")).\\n\\nIn Jämtland the Scandinavian inland transhumance, *buföring*, has always been more important than cultivation. In fact it was crucial to take care of the livestock and supply them with food, and rewarding. Every summer for several weeks, from May to September, *gjetaran* (herd boys) and *butøusan* (herd girls, *bu* is cognate to \"booth\") followed and guarded *kreka*, the critter, on their way to a [grazing land](/wiki/Grazing \"Grazing\") on higher altitudes where several critter houses had been raised. The common animals taken out on these journeys were *gjettran* (Jämtland goats) and *kynnan* (the fell cows) a white, brisk and headstrong cow race, lacking horns. It was a hard work and it depended on cooperation between males and females. This lifestyle lived on for thousand years and it was first in the 1950s it became obsolete. This tradition has however been resurrected as of late, mostly for touristic purposes.\\n\\nWhen the population settled down the society greatly changed, first coexisting with the older societies, later absorbing them. Trade became much more important, a political institution elected by the people came into existence, the very same institution whose successor is the current County Council. Jämtland got its name and a somewhat [hierarchical](/wiki/Hierarchy \"Hierarchy\") social structure emerged, though, as already pointed out, Jämtland never had an upper class. Strong families such as [Skanke](/wiki/Skanke \"Skanke\") and [Blix](/w/index.php?title=Blix_(noble_family)&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Blix (noble family) (page does not exist)\") did exist though and on the countryside in Jämtland people still live in networks of relatives, *families*. Where they provide a second [social security](/wiki/Social_security \"Social security\") for many, in the rest of Sweden and in e.g. Östersund this has completely or almost entirely been replaced by [public welfare](/wiki/Public_welfare \"Public welfare\").\\n\\n### Cuisine\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=22 \"Edit section: Cuisine\")]\\n\\nSee also: [Cuisine of Norway](/wiki/Cuisine_of_Norway \"Cuisine of Norway\") and [Cuisine of Sweden](/wiki/Cuisine_of_Sweden \"Cuisine of Sweden\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Messmor.jpg/250px-Messmor.jpg)](/wiki/File:Messmor.jpg)\\n\\n*Messmör*, soft whey butter, is a Jamtish product popular in Sweden\\n\\nMuch of Jämtland\\'s cuisine is remnant from the herding stage. Just like other Scandinavians, it is common among Jamts to drink [milk](/wiki/Milk \"Milk\") throughout their entire life. There are many different types of Jamtish [dairy products](/wiki/Dairy_products \"Dairy products\"), especially cheese, since it was by far the easiest way to conserve milk. [Mesost](/wiki/Brunost \"Brunost\") is particularly associated with Jämtland and also e.g. a local variant of [cottage cheese](/wiki/Cottage_cheese \"Cottage cheese\") called *grynost*. In Jämtland there are several small [dairies](/wiki/Dairy \"Dairy\") in the villages, most famous is the one in [Skärvången](/w/index.php?title=Sk%C3%A4rv%C3%A5ngen&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Skärvången (page does not exist)\"). Other products associated with Jämtland are the [soft whey butter](/w/index.php?title=Soft_whey_butter&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Soft whey butter (page does not exist)\"), [long fil](/w/index.php?title=Long_fil&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Long fil (page does not exist)\"), [kjesfil](/w/index.php?title=Kjesfil&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Kjesfil (page does not exist)\"), *flautgröt* \"[cream](/wiki/Cream \"Cream\") [porridge](/wiki/Porridge \"Porridge\")\", [tunnbröd](/wiki/Tunnbr%C3%B6d \"Tunnbröd\"), a version of [palt](/wiki/Palt \"Palt\") called *kams*, klobb etc.\\n\\nThe ancient practice of brewing *Julöl* (yule beer) persists even today with the [microbrewery](/wiki/Microbrewery \"Microbrewery\") [Jämtlands Bryggeri](/wiki/J%C3%A4mtlands_Bryggeri \"Jämtlands Bryggeri\") in [Pilgrimstad](/wiki/Pilgrimstad \"Pilgrimstad\").\\n\\nLocal projects such as the internet portal [Food of Jämtland](http://www.foodofjamtland.se/english) and the trading mark *[Smakriket Jämtland](https://www.smakriket.se)* (the \"taste realm\" Jämtland) are two major contributors in marketing, preserving and developing the cuisine of Jämtland.\\n\\nSome of the newest merchandises in Jämtland are a [sparkling wine](/wiki/Sparkling_wine \"Sparkling wine\") made of [birch](/wiki/Birch \"Birch\") [sap](/wiki/Sap \"Sap\") and a [sausage](/wiki/Sausage \"Sausage\") called *Jämtlandsfalu*, wilderness juice, the [snaps](/wiki/Snaps \"Snaps\") *kallsup* and tunnbröd [chips.](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/chips \"wikt:chips\")\\n\\n### Folklore\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=23 \"Edit section: Folklore\")]\\n\\nSee also: [Scandinavian folklore](/wiki/Scandinavian_folklore \"Scandinavian folklore\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/PB190187.JPG/250px-PB190187.JPG)](/wiki/File:PB190187.JPG)\\n\\nLake Storsjön\\n\\nThe folklore of Jämtland mostly correspond to [Scandinavian folklore](/wiki/Scandinavian_folklore \"Scandinavian folklore\") as whole, although the folklore is seldom regarded as popular belief nowadays, with one major exception, [Storsjöodjuret](/wiki/Storsj%C3%B6odjuret \"Storsjöodjuret\").\\n\\nAccording to legend it is believed that [Storsjön](/wiki/Storsj%C3%B6n \"Storsjön\") (literally *the Great Lake*) harbors a large lake creature, Storsjöodjuret. There are many witness reports but the creature\\'s existence remains to be established conclusively. Regardless of any proven existence, Storsjöodjuret was officially placed under the protection of a degree issued in 1986 by the [County Administrative Board](/wiki/County_Administrative_Boards_of_Sweden \"County Administrative Boards of Sweden\") to guarantee its safety from hunters and fortune seekers, the protection was lifted in November 2005.[[27]](#cite_note-27) The first description of Storsjöodjuret was made in this tale from 1635;\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg/250px-Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg)](/wiki/File:Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg)\\n\\nStorsjöodjuret is commonly represented by this figure.\\n\\n\\n> A long, long time ago two trolls, Jata and Kata, stood on the shores of the Great Lake brewing a concoction in their cauldrons. They brewed and mixed and added to the liquid for days and weeks and years. They knew not what would result from their brew but they wondered about it a great deal. One evening there was heard a strange sound from one of their cauldrons. There was a wailing, a groaning and a crying, then suddenly came a loud bang. A strange animal with a black serpentine body and a cat-like head jumped out of the cauldron and disappeared into the lake. The monster enjoyed living in the lake, grew unbelievably larger and awakened terror among the people whenever it appeared. Finally, it extended all the way round the island of Frösön, and could even bite its own tail. Ketil Runske bound the mighty monster with a strong spell which was carved on a stone and raised on the island of Frösön. The serpent was pictured on the stone. Thus was the spell to be tied till the day someone came who could read and understand the inscription on the stone.\\n\\n*[Puken](/w/index.php?title=Puken&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Puken (page does not exist)\")* is a magical ball of [yarn](/wiki/Yarn \"Yarn\") summoned by a witch to draw objects to her. It often steals milk to the witch by milking [cows](/wiki/Cow \"Cow\").[[28]](#cite_note-28)\\n\\nJust like in the rest of the world [dragons](/wiki/Dragon \"Dragon\") have been known for a long time. In Jämtland they resemble [brooms](/wiki/Broom \"Broom\"), that flies quickly and strikes down where [treasuries](/wiki/Treasury \"Treasury\") are buried.[[29]](#cite_note-29)\\n\\n*[Sjörå](/wiki/Sj%C3%B6r%C3%A5 \"Sjörå\")* is a keeper of freshwater, that master fish, [aas](/wiki/River \"River\") and lakes. It is similar to the Jamtish *[skogskjæringa](/wiki/Hulder \"Hulder\")* \"wife of the forest\". A being that, at day, takes the appearance of a *[rauvtjuksa](/wiki/Siberian_jay \"Siberian jay\")* \"red tail\", a bird seen as ominous in Jamtish folklore. When in physical form her tail is always apparent. She tries to lure men to have [sexual intercourse](/wiki/Sexual_intercourse \"Sexual intercourse\") with her. The *skogsrå* is not the same creature as skogskjæringa in Jamtish folklore, it is the keeper of the forest and master all the animals in it. It takes on the shape of a moose during hunting season, and grows larger and larger if hit by bullets and eventually forces the hunters out. It can however, be slain with a silver bullet.[[30]](#cite_note-30)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Johan_Tirens_naecken.jpg/250px-Johan_Tirens_naecken.jpg)](/wiki/File:Johan_Tirens_naecken.jpg)\\n\\nLocal artist [Johan Tirén](/wiki/Johan_Tir%C3%A9n \"Johan Tirén\")\\'s painting *Jämtlandssägen* (Jämtland\\'s tale) with a young fiddler wearing traditional Great Jamtish clothes, whilst listening to the Nix play.\\n\\n[Tomten](/wiki/Tomte \"Tomte\") is a common creature, it is quite tall and has an eye in the middle of his forehead. It is the keeper of [barns](/wiki/Barn \"Barn\") and a very capricious being, though he usually brings luck.[[31]](#cite_note-p_98-31)\\n\\nThe [Nix](/wiki/Neck_(water_spirit) \"Neck (water spirit)\"), *Näkkjen*, is a common mythical creature, in Jämtland it refers to a male water spirit whose music was dangerous to women. Each year in the town of [Hackås](/wiki/Hack%C3%A5s \"Hackås\") in southern Jämtland an annual [traditional music](/wiki/Traditional_Nordic_dance_music \"Traditional Nordic dance music\") contest *[Årets Näck](/wiki/%C3%85rets_N%C3%A4ck \"Årets Näck\")* is held where each contestant impersonates the Nix.\\n\\nIn Jämtland the [vættir](/wiki/V%C3%A6ttir \"Vættir\")/[dwarves](/wiki/Dwarf_(mythology) \"Dwarf (mythology)\") goes by the name *jolbyggar* \"earth builders\". They herd large white goats and cows and live underground, they are considered innocuous though sometimes they exchange an unbaptized child for a so-called *bytningsbarn*. They are commonly associated with the grazing lands.[[31]](#cite_note-p_98-31) They also go by the names *småruskan*, *smågubban* and *småtussan*.\\n\\n### Folk costumes\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=24 \"Edit section: Folk costumes\")]\\n\\nJämtland has several different types of folk costumes or *[bunads](/wiki/Bunad \"Bunad\")*. Unlike certain regions in Scandinavia a unitary bunad did not exist in Jämtland\\'s parishes, with the exception of [Hammerdal parish](/w/index.php?title=Hammerdal_parish&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Hammerdal parish (page does not exist)\") with its [brown](/wiki/Brown \"Brown\")-striped clothing.\\n\\nUsually Jämtland is divided into three different clothing parts, the North Jamtish ([Hammerdal](/wiki/Hammerdal_Court_District \"Hammerdal Court District\")), the East Jamtish ([Ragunda](/wiki/Ragunda_Court_District \"Ragunda Court District\")) and the Great Jamtish area, covering the rest and the majority of Jämtland.\\n\\nThe North Jamtish clothing part is typically influenced by the folk costumes of northern Ångermanland and to a lesser degree Lapland, with the exception of [Frostviken parish](/w/index.php?title=Frostviken_parish&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Frostviken parish (page does not exist)\") settled by [Trønders](/wiki/Tr%C3%B8ndersk \"Trøndersk\") in the 18th century. The East Jamtish part is the least old-fashioned of the three with many changes done to the costumes through time, making them closer to the kind used at the Swedish coast, rather than the others in Jämtland. The Great Jamtish part has typically old-fashioned and conservative homogeneous bunads with blue socks, red knitted caps among the males, dark bounded caps for ladies and coloured for girls. The skirts are usually of a single colour and the men have blue or black [hodden](/wiki/Hodden \"Hodden\") [coats](/wiki/Coat_(clothing) \"Coat (clothing)\"), with yellow [chamois leather](/wiki/Chamois_leather \"Chamois leather\") pants made from moose skin.\\n\\n### Dialects\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=25 \"Edit section: Dialects\")]\\n\\nThe genuine dialect of Jämtland is [Jamtish](/wiki/Jamtish \"Jamtish\"). The speakers of the dialect refer to it as *Jamska* ([ˈjamskɐ]), which is a definite form that translates to English as \"the Jamtish\". However, due to the lack of a well-established English name of the dialect both Jamtish and Jamtlandic are used.\\n\\nJamtish is in fact a group of dialects and there are distinctive dialects in every parish. Though they are usually classified in four groups; *framlänningsmålet* \"the Central Jamtish tongue\", *opplänningsmålet* (spoken in Western Jämtland), Southwest Jamtish and Northern Jamtish. The dialects in eastern Jämtland are sometimes considered as a fifth group of Jamtish, but also as dialects more related to the Swedish dialects spoken in [Ångermanland](/wiki/%C3%85ngermanland \"Ångermanland\"). In the very north of Jämtland *lidmål*, a version of [Trøndersk](/wiki/Tr%C3%B8ndersk \"Trøndersk\"), is spoken. Jamtish is spoken by 50 000 people at most living in Jämtland and in other areas of Sweden, particularly the capital [Stockholm](/wiki/Stockholm \"Stockholm\").\\n\\n|  |  |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| *Veit vår gräse ahllten e, brano grönt*  *å grönar tre, veit vår all får væ i fre?*  *Veit vår ingenting e svårst*  *å e öft, e huskut kort*  *om nättran er e lagom mårt?*  *De e västa nola værln*  *å åsta sönna hagan*  *nola västa sjön*  *å sönna åsta dagom*  - From [Triakel](/wiki/Triakel \"Triakel\")\\'s song **Veit**[[32]](#cite_note-32) | *Where d\\'you find a life of ease, green grass*   *and greener trees, gently waving in the breeze?*  *Where d\\'you think the bugs don\\'t bite*  *And the work, as quick and light?*  *Where\\'s it hardly dark at night?*  *It\\'s to the east of the waning moon*  *And to the west of the wide horizon,*  *North of where the sun goes down*  *And south of where it\\'s rising.*   English version of the same song, though not a literal translation. |\\n\\n### Language\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=26 \"Edit section: Language\")]\\n\\nEven if the Jamtish official status is a dialect many Jamtish people see it as an own language. There are multiple activists that are trying to make the Swedish government recognise Jamtish as a minority language just as [Yiddish](/wiki/Yiddish \"Yiddish\") or [Sami](/wiki/Sami_people \"Sami people\") have become one. The claimers say to look at the different words and pronunciations of them. Whether or not it is its own language has been widely debated since the early 20th century.\\n\\n### Provincial character\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=27 \"Edit section: Provincial character\")]\\n\\nHistorically each province in Sweden has been known for a specific provincial character or *[volksgeist](/wiki/Volksgeist \"Volksgeist\")*. This was a field of intense research in Sweden earlier but is viewed somewhat unmodern and considered prejudice today.\\n\\nThe provincial character of Jämtland was often portrayed as cheerful and the population have historically been known for their hospitality. Before the dawn of the railway it was common among farmers to leave their doors unlocked when the annual summer journey to the critter houses was due, often with the table set with food for travelers.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Ostersund.JPG/250px-Ostersund.JPG)](/wiki/File:Ostersund.JPG)\\n\\nÖstersund was founded to stop the faring traditions in Jämtland. This happened first after the railroad was established and the city is now the trading center of Jämtland.\\n\\nThe faring traditions of Jämtland are also very characteristic. The Jamts were known to neglect the agriculture and instead take on long trading journeys all over Scandinavia to various [markets](/wiki/Market_(place) \"Market (place)\") such as the ancients ones in [Levanger](/wiki/Levanger_(town) \"Levanger (town)\") and [Gregorius market](/w/index.php?title=Gregorius_market&action=edit&redlink=1 \"Gregorius market (page does not exist)\") on Frösön. This was regarded as sheer pleasure in itself and not as something they were obligated to do. In the middle of the 18th century Jämtland\\'s population was roughly 20 000 and it was common that over 1 000 Jamts were present during *Marsimartnan* in Levanger, it is also claimed that the city was built solely on spikes from Jämtland before the fire in the 19th century. The journeys took place during the winters when the landscape was more accessible (when [swamps](/wiki/Swamp \"Swamp\"), lakes and [tarns](/wiki/Tarn_(lake) \"Tarn (lake)\") froze to ice) and was conducted by males, which left the females in complete charge of the [household](/wiki/Household \"Household\") and the [property](/wiki/Property \"Property\"). The journeys were well-organized [expeditions](/wiki/Exploration \"Exploration\") and no one traveled alone. These traditions has awarded the Jamt with traits such as enterprising and energetic. The Jamts\\' attempts to avoid tariffs were very successful which greatly angered Swedish officials through time. These journeys eventually stopped once the railway came, though it has recently been renewed by locals. Some say that the heritage from this age lives on, given the high number of enterprises per capita.\\n\\n### Republic of Jamtland\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=28 \"Edit section: Republic of Jamtland\")]\\n\\nMain article: [Republic of Jamtland](/wiki/Republic_of_Jamtland \"Republic of Jamtland\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg/250px-Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg)\\n\\n[Flag of the Republic of Jamtland](/wiki/Flag_of_the_Republic_of_Jamtland \"Flag of the Republic of Jamtland\")\\n\\nIn the 1960s, an [independence movement](/wiki/Independence_movement \"Independence movement\") calling itself the \"Republic of Jamtland\" was created by humorist/actor/director [Yngve Gamlin](/wiki/Yngve_Gamlin \"Yngve Gamlin\"). Motivated on paper as an attempt to return the province to Jamtlandic control, the republic was given some form of recognition in 1967 when Mr. Gamlin was invited to an event for visiting statesmen hosted by Swedish prime minister [Tage Erlander](/wiki/Tage_Erlander \"Tage Erlander\"). Described in some sources as a form of criticism against [centralized](/wiki/Centralized \"Centralized\") Swedish government and in others as a [marketing](/wiki/Marketing \"Marketing\") ploy, it is likely that both played some part in its foundation (Republic officials typically describe it as \"51 percent serious\"). The republic has a self-styled [flag](/wiki/Flag_of_the_Republic_of_Jamtland \"Flag of the Republic of Jamtland\") and national anthem ([Jämtlandssången](/wiki/J%C3%A4mtlandss%C3%A5ngen \"Jämtlandssången\")) and the independence movement hosts the annual [Storsjöyran](/wiki/Storsj%C3%B6yran \"Storsjöyran\") event in the capital, [Östersund](/wiki/%C3%96stersund \"Östersund\").\\n\\n### Sports\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=29 \"Edit section: Sports\")]\\n\\nFootball in the province is administered by [Jämtland-Härjedalens Fotbollförbund](/wiki/J%C3%A4mtland-H%C3%A4rjedalens_Fotbollf%C3%B6rbund \"Jämtland-Härjedalens Fotbollförbund\"). [SE322](http://dd.eionet.europa.eu/vocabularyconcept/common/nuts/SE322) |\\n| Website | [www.z.lst.se](http://www.z.lst.se) |\\n\\n**Jämtland County** ([Swedish](/wiki/Swedish_language \"Swedish language\"): *Jämtlands län*, [Southern Sami](/wiki/Southern_Sami_language \"Southern Sami language\"): *Jiemthen leene*) is a [county](/wiki/Counties_of_Sweden \"Counties of Sweden\") or *[län](/wiki/L%C3%A4n \"Län\")* in [Sweden](/wiki/Sweden \"Sweden\"). It consists of the provinces of [Jämtland](/wiki/J%C3%A4mtland \"Jämtland\") and [Härjedalen](/wiki/H%C3%A4rjedalen \"Härjedalen\"), along with minor parts of [Hälsingland](/wiki/H%C3%A4lsingland \"Hälsingland\") and [Ångermanland](/wiki/%C3%85ngermanland \"Ångermanland\"), plus two small strips of [Lapland](/wiki/Lapland,_Sweden \"Lapland, Sweden\") and [Dalarna](/wiki/Dalarna \"Dalarna\"). It borders the counties of [Dalarna](/wiki/Dalarna_County \"Dalarna County\"), [Gävleborg](/wiki/G%C3%A4vleborg_County \"Gävleborg County\"), [Västernorrland](/wiki/V%C3%A4sternorrland_County \"Västernorrland County\"), and [Västerbotten](/wiki/V%C3%A4sterbotten_County \"Västerbotten County\"), as well as the Norwegian county of [Trøndelag](/wiki/Tr%C3%B8ndelag \"Trøndelag\"). It measures 49,443\\xa0km2 (19,090\\xa0sq\\xa0mi) and constitutes 12% of Sweden\\'s total area, making it the country\\'s third largest county. The capital is [Östersund](/wiki/%C3%96stersund \"Östersund\"). The [county governor](/wiki/List_of_governors_of_J%C3%A4mtland_County \"List of governors of Jämtland County\") and leader of the [administrative board](/wiki/County_Administrative_Boards_of_Sweden \"County Administrative Boards of Sweden\"), as appointed by the Swedish government, has been Marita Ljung since 2021.[[3]](#cite_note-3)\\n\\nThe county was established in 1810, at the time it consisted only of the provinces of Jämtland and Härjedalen, which is why the [coat of arms](/wiki/Coat_of_arms \"Coat of arms\") is a shield parted per fess with their provincial arms. [King Carl XVI Gustaf](/wiki/Carl_XVI_Gustaf \"Carl XVI Gustaf\") is occasionally referred to as Duke of Jämtland after his title of king.\\n\\nProvince\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland_County&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Province\")]\\n\\nFor history, geography and culture, see [Jämtland](/wiki/J%C3%A4mtland \"Jämtland\") and [Härjedalen](/wiki/H%C3%A4rjedalen \"Härjedalen\").\\n\\nJämtland County consists of primarily the provinces of Jämtland and Härjedalen, though minor parts of [Hälsingland](/wiki/H%C3%A4lsingland \"Hälsingland\") and [Ångermanland](/wiki/%C3%85ngermanland \"Ångermanland\") are also included, along with small uninhabited areas in [Lapland](/wiki/Lapland,_Sweden \"Lapland, Sweden\") and [Dalarna](/wiki/Dalarna \"Dalarna\").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nAdministration\\n--------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland_County&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Administration\")]\\n\\nThe main aim of the [County Administrative Board](/wiki/County_Administrative_Boards_of_Sweden \"County Administrative Boards of Sweden\") is to fulfill the goals set in national politics by the [Riksdag](/wiki/Riksdag \"Riksdag\") and the [Government](/wiki/Government_of_Sweden \"Government of Sweden\"), to coordinate the interests and promote the development of the county, to establish regional goals and safeguard the due process of law in the handling of each case. The County Administrative Board is a [Government Agency](/wiki/Government_Agencies_in_Sweden \"Government Agencies in Sweden\") headed by a Governor. See [List of Jämtland Governors](/wiki/List_of_J%C3%A4mtland_Governors \"List of Jämtland Governors\").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nDemography\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland_County&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Demography\")]\\n\\nJämtland County is sparsely populated and more than one-third of the population lives in the [countryside](/wiki/Countryside \"Countryside\"), making Jämtland County the second largest rural region in Sweden, after [Gotland County](/wiki/Gotland_County \"Gotland County\"). However, most of the population lives in the rather densely populated region surrounding lake [Storsjön](/wiki/Storsj%C3%B6n \"Storsjön\"), commonly called *Storsjöbygden*, \"the Storsjö district/countryside\".[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nPolitics\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland_County&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: Politics\")]\\n\\nThe county is dominated by the [Swedish Social Democratic Party](/wiki/Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party \"Swedish Social Democratic Party\") and the [Centre Party](/wiki/Centre_Party_(Sweden) \"Centre Party (Sweden)\"), which is unique in Sweden, but corresponds to the situation in the bordering Norwegian county of Nord-Trøndelag. The county is rather contrastive in the political field. While a majority of the municipalities are governed by [liberal](/wiki/Liberalism \"Liberalism\")-[conservative](/wiki/Conservatism \"Conservatism\") ([Swedish](/wiki/Swedish_language \"Swedish language\"): *borgerlig*, lit. \"[bourgeois](/wiki/Bourgeois \"Bourgeois\")\") majorities or by coalitions overstepping the bloc border, the [county council](/wiki/County_Councils_of_Sweden \"County Councils of Sweden\") is controlled by a [red-green](/wiki/Red-Greens_(Sweden) \"Red-Greens (Sweden)\") majority and the Social Democrats receive two out of four [mandates](/wiki/Mandate_(politics) \"Mandate (politics)\") to the [Riksdag](/wiki/Riksdag \"Riksdag\").\\n\\nAfter the Swedish county council election in 2022, the following [political parties](/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Sweden \"List of political parties in Sweden\") are represented in the Jämtland county council ([Swedish](/wiki/Swedish_language \"Swedish language\"): *Region Jämtland Härjedalen*):[[4]](#cite_note-4)\\n\\n| Party | | Seats | Votes | % |\\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\\n|  | [Social Democrats](/wiki/Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party \"Swedish Social Democratic Party\") | 21 | 30,702 | 36.95% |\\n|  | [Moderate Party](/wiki/Moderate_Party \"Moderate Party\") | 9 | 12,941 | 15.57% |\\n|  | [Centre Party](/wiki/Centre_Party_(Sweden) \"Centre Party (Sweden)\") | 7 | 10,486 | 12.62% |\\n|  | [Sweden Democrats](/wiki/Sweden_Democrats \"Sweden Democrats\") | 7 | 10,343 | 12.45% |\\n|  | [Christian Democrats](/wiki/Christian_Democrats_(Sweden) \"Christian Democrats (Sweden)\") | 5 | 7,280 | 8.76% |\\n|  | [Left Party](/wiki/Left_Party_(Sweden) \"Left Party (Sweden)\") | 4 | 5,992 | 7.21% |\\n|  | [Green Party](/wiki/Green_Party_(Sweden) \"Green Party (Sweden)\") | 2 | 2,688 | 3.23% |\\n|  | [Liberals](/wiki/Liberals_(Sweden) \"Liberals (Sweden)\") | - **Debbie Kilroy** [OAM](/wiki/Medal_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Medal of the Order of Australia") (born 1961), née **Deborah Harding**, is an Australian [human rights activist](/wiki/Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist") and [prison reformer](/wiki/Prison_reform "Prison reform"). She is known for having founded [Sisters Inside](/wiki/Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside"), an independent community organisation based in [Queensland](/wiki/Queensland "Queensland"), Australia, that advocates for the human rights of women and girls in the [criminal legal system](/wiki/Criminal_law "Criminal law"). She is a qualified lawyer, who in 2007 was the first person with serious convictions to be allowed to practise law by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland").

Early life and education
------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Deborah[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1) Harding[[2]](#cite_note-wmoa-2) was born in 1961 in [Brisbane](/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane"), and raised in the suburb of [Kedron](/wiki/Kedron,_Queensland "Kedron, Queensland"), Queensland. During her teens, she became rebellious, and, after being locked up at the age of 14 for a four-week psychiatric assessment, began a period of increasing criminalisation and imprisonment, with only brief periods out of the [criminal justice system](/wiki/Criminal_justice_system "Criminal justice system") during her teens. Witnessing and being a victim of injustices within the system, her early experiences with it made her angry.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)

She had a child at the age of 18, and endured a [violent relationship](/wiki/Domestic_violence "Domestic violence") for some years. After leaving that relationship she met and in 1986 married her present husband, [rugby league](/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league") footballer [Joe Kilroy](/wiki/Joe_Kilroy "Joe Kilroy"), and they had a child together. Debbie was sentenced to six years in prison[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3) after having sold [cannabis](/wiki/Cannabis "Cannabis") to undercover police.[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1)

In 1990, she witnessed her friend Debbie Dick being murdered in the overcrowded [Boggo Road Gaol](/wiki/Boggo_Road_Gaol "Boggo Road Gaol"),[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4) and has said that "[her] commitment to fight against the criminalisation and imprisonment of women is in honour of her memory and the memories of all the women and girls who have died at the hands of the prison industrial complex". As a result of this murder, the prison authorities started involving prisoners in committees that helped to run the prison.[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1)

During the three years that she served of her sentence before her release in 1992, she began training as a [social worker](/wiki/Social_worker "Social worker") through the [University of Queensland](/wiki/University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"), determined to improve the situation of women and children in prison.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

Sisters Inside
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Sisters Inside")]

Upon her release from prison in 1992, Kilroy started to establish Sisters Inside, an organisation dedicated to responding to the needs and human rights of criminalised women and the children affected by their imprisonment that were not being met by available services. At first Sisters Inside was a small group run mostly by volunteers, but it has grown into a larger community-based organisation providing a range of services to many women and children in Queensland.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3) Author [Melissa Lucashenko](/wiki/Melissa_Lucashenko "Melissa Lucashenko") is a founding member.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

The motto of Sisters Inside is "nothing about us without us".[[6]](#cite_note-shedefined-6)

Career
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

Kilroy completed her legal training as well as a Graduate Diploma in Forensic Mental Health (she is trained in [gestalt therapy](/wiki/Gestalt_therapy "Gestalt therapy")[[2]](#cite_note-wmoa-2)), and in 2017 was the first former prisoner to be admitted as a [legal practitioner](/wiki/Legal_practitioner "Legal practitioner") by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland"),[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3) a decision ruled by Justice [Paul de Jersey](/wiki/Paul_de_Jersey "Paul de Jersey"), future [chief justice](/wiki/Chief_justice_of_Queensland "Chief justice of Queensland") and later [governor of Queensland](/wiki/Governor_of_Queensland "Governor of Queensland").[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

She opened her own legal practice in 2013.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Kilroy has served as an Executive Member of the [Queensland Council for Civil Liberties](/wiki/Queensland_Council_for_Civil_Liberties "Queensland Council for Civil Liberties") since 2001 and [ex-officio](/wiki/Ex-officio "Ex-officio") chairperson of the Youth Affairs Network of Queensland since 1997 (As of 2019[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit)). She has also served a member of a number of other bodies and organisations, including:[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)

* the Criminal Law Committee;
* [Law Council of Australia](/wiki/Law_Council_of_Australia "Law Council of Australia")
* Criminal Law Committee, [Queensland Law Society](/wiki/Queensland_Law_Society "Queensland Law Society")
* Equal Rights Alliance
* Australian Women Again Violence Alliance
* National Coronial Reform, [Federation of Community Legal Centres](/wiki/Community_legal_centre "Community legal centre")
* Criminal Justice Network

She has been appointed to state and national working groups on a range of legal and social issues, and has also contributed to international forums, such as meetings convened by the [UN Office on Drugs and Crime](/wiki/UN_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime "UN Office on Drugs and Crime") to develop draft UN Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-Custodial Measures for Women Offenders; sessions of the Commission on the Status of Women; and conferences on [crime prevention](/wiki/Crime_prevention "Crime prevention") and criminal justice.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)

In November 2016 Kilroy was appointed to Queensland's Sentencing Advisory Council.[[8]](#cite_note-8) She believes that the council has an important role to play in educating the public, to counteract the "law-and-order hysteria" seen in the media and spruiked by politicians.[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

In early 2019, she led a [crowd-funding](/wiki/Crowd-funding "Crowd-funding") campaign called #freeher to pay off the court debts of Indigenous women in [Western Australia](/wiki/Western_Australia "Western Australia") who had been imprisoned for defaulting on fines, raising over A$400,000 and enabling the release of 11 women.[[9]](#cite_note-ausstory-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) Amendments to the WA legislation were passed in 2020, partly as result of the recommendation from the coronial inquiry into the [death of Ms Dhu](/wiki/Death_of_Ms_Dhu "Death of Ms Dhu"), who [died in police custody](/wiki/Aboriginal_deaths_in_custody "Aboriginal deaths in custody").[[11]](#cite_note-11)

In April 2020 Kilroy contracted [COVID-19](/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") after travelling to the United States with her friend and colleague Boneeta-Marie Mabo, with both becoming so unwell that they were admitted to hospital.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Around 18 months of contracting the virus, in September 2021, she was still suffering from [Long COVID](/wiki/Long_COVID "Long COVID"), with a debilitating range of symptoms.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

As of 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit) she is principal of the law firm Kilroy & Callaghan, where she leads a team of five, and [CEO](/wiki/CEO "CEO") of Sisters Inside. She is passionate about encouraging former offenders, and in particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and [culturally diverse](/wiki/Multiculturalism_in_Australia#Terminology "Multiculturalism in Australia") women to become criminal lawyers.[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1)

Beliefs and advocacy
--------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Beliefs and advocacy")]

Kilroy's experience of imprisonment led to her belief that unnecessary trauma caused by the prison system, including [solitary confinement](/wiki/Solitary_confinement "Solitary confinement") as a punishment for [self-harm](/wiki/Self-harm "Self-harm"), leads to a greater likelihood of women re-offending and ending up back in prison.[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1) Influenced by people such as the US academic, activist and former prisoner [Angela Davis](/wiki/Angela_Davis "Angela Davis"), Kilroy believes that the prison system fails in its mission to punish and rehabilitate, with more than half of women released from prison returning to spend another stint there.[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She names two other former prisoners as heroes of hers: [Nelson Mandela](/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi")[[14]](#cite_note-14)

She has said that there is a need to break down "racism, misogyny and sexism within the legal frameworks", and that harsher sentences are not the answer.[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She points out that "The vast majority of women prisoners are imprisoned for minor, non-violent crimes... [which] are often poverty-related", with around 40% being [onremand](/wiki/Remand_(detention) "Remand (detention)"), as yet untried for their alleged crimes. She says:[[6]](#cite_note-shedefined-6)

> Too often women are imprisoned on remand for failures of the state. Failure to provide adequate income support, to support women leaving violent homes, to provide essential housing and health services, and to address multigenerational harm arising from colonisation.

She engages in public debate and advocates for women on a range of issues, including violence, [homelessness](/wiki/Homelessness "Homelessness"), [racism](/wiki/Racism_in_Australia "Racism in Australia"), mental health, [substance abuse](/wiki/Substance_abuse "Substance abuse"), poverty, [child protection](/wiki/Child_protection "Child protection"), sexual assault, and failures in government systems. She aims to reduce the rate of criminalisation and imprisonment of women and children, in particular the over-representation of [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander](/wiki/Aboriginal_and_Torres_Strait_Islander "Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander") within the criminal justice system, and to women reduce the impact of mothers' imprisonment on their children.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)

Recognition
-----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recognition")]

* 2003: [Order of Australia Medal](/wiki/Order_of_Australia_Medal "Order of Australia Medal")[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2004: [Australian Human Rights Medal](/wiki/Australian_Human_Rights_Medal "Australian Human Rights Medal")[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Emergent Woman Lawyer of the Year[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Peace Women Award[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2014: [Churchill Fellowship](/wiki/Churchill_Fellowship "Churchill Fellowship")[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2016: shortlisted Queensland nomination for [Australian of the Year](/wiki/Australian_of_the_Year "Australian of the Year")[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2019: keynote speaker at the [Law Institute of Victoria](/wiki/Law_Institute_of_Victoria "Law Institute of Victoria")'s Women in Leadership lunch[[15]](#cite_note-15)
* 2019: [Voltaire Human Rights Award](/wiki/Voltaire_Human_Rights_Award "Voltaire Human Rights Award")[[16]](#cite_note-16)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Australian human rights activist and prison reformer

| Debbie Kilroy | |
| --- | --- |
| Born | Deborah Harding  1961 (age 64–65)  [Brisbane](/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane"), [Queensland](/wiki/Queensland "Queensland"), Australia |
| Education | . [University of Queensland](/wiki/University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland") |
| Occupations | [Human rights activist](/wiki/Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist"), [prison reformer](/wiki/Prison_reform "Prison reform"), lawyer |
| Years active | 1992–present |
| Known for | Founder of [Sisters Inside](/wiki/Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside") |
| Spouse | [Joe Kilroy](/wiki/Joe_Kilroy "Joe Kilroy") |

**Debbie Kilroy** [OAM](/wiki/Medal_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Medal of the Order of Australia") (born 1961), née **Deborah Harding**, is an Australian [human rights activist](/wiki/Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist") and [prison reformer](/wiki/Prison_reform "Prison reform"). She is known for having founded [Sisters Inside](/wiki/Sisters_Inside "Sisters Inside"), an independent community organisation based in [Queensland](/wiki/Queensland "Queensland"), Australia, that advocates for the human rights of women and girls in the [criminal legal system](/wiki/Criminal_law "Criminal law"). She is a qualified lawyer, who in 2007 was the first person with serious convictions to be allowed to practise law by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland").

Early life and education
------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Deborah[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1) Harding[[2]](#cite_note-wmoa-2) was born in 1961 in [Brisbane](/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane"), and raised in the suburb of [Kedron](/wiki/Kedron,_Queensland "Kedron, Queensland"), Queensland. During her teens, she became rebellious, and, after being locked up at the age of 14 for a four-week psychiatric assessment, began a period of increasing criminalisation and imprisonment, with only brief periods out of the [criminal justice system](/wiki/Criminal_justice_system "Criminal justice system") during her teens. Witnessing and being a victim of injustices within the system, her early experiences with it made her angry.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)

She had a child at the age of 18, and endured a [violent relationship](/wiki/Domestic_violence "Domestic violence") for some years. After leaving that relationship she met and in 1986 married her present husband, [rugby league](/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league") footballer [Joe Kilroy](/wiki/Joe_Kilroy "Joe Kilroy"), and they had a child together. Debbie was sentenced to six years in prison[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3) after having sold [cannabis](/wiki/Cannabis "Cannabis") to undercover police.[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1)

In 1990, she witnessed her friend Debbie Dick being murdered in the overcrowded [Boggo Road Gaol](/wiki/Boggo_Road_Gaol "Boggo Road Gaol"),[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4) and has said that "[her] commitment to fight against the criminalisation and imprisonment of women is in honour of her memory and the memories of all the women and girls who have died at the hands of the prison industrial complex". As a result of this murder, the prison authorities started involving prisoners in committees that helped to run the prison.[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1)

During the three years that she served of her sentence before her release in 1992, she began training as a [social worker](/wiki/Social_worker "Social worker") through the [University of Queensland](/wiki/University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"), determined to improve the situation of women and children in prison.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

Sisters Inside
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Sisters Inside")]

Upon her release from prison in 1992, Kilroy started to establish Sisters Inside, an organisation dedicated to responding to the needs and human rights of criminalised women and the children affected by their imprisonment that were not being met by available services. At first Sisters Inside was a small group run mostly by volunteers, but it has grown into a larger community-based organisation providing a range of services to many women and children in Queensland.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3) Author [Melissa Lucashenko](/wiki/Melissa_Lucashenko "Melissa Lucashenko") is a founding member.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

The motto of Sisters Inside is "nothing about us without us".[[6]](#cite_note-shedefined-6)

Career
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

Kilroy completed her legal training as well as a Graduate Diploma in Forensic Mental Health (she is trained in [gestalt therapy](/wiki/Gestalt_therapy "Gestalt therapy")[[2]](#cite_note-wmoa-2)), and in 2017 was the first former prisoner to be admitted as a [legal practitioner](/wiki/Legal_practitioner "Legal practitioner") by the [Supreme Court of Queensland](/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Queensland "Supreme Court of Queensland"),[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3) a decision ruled by Justice [Paul de Jersey](/wiki/Paul_de_Jersey "Paul de Jersey"), future [chief justice](/wiki/Chief_justice_of_Queensland "Chief justice of Queensland") and later [governor of Queensland](/wiki/Governor_of_Queensland "Governor of Queensland").[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

She opened her own legal practice in 2013.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Kilroy has served as an Executive Member of the [Queensland Council for Civil Liberties](/wiki/Queensland_Council_for_Civil_Liberties "Queensland Council for Civil Liberties") since 2001 and [ex-officio](/wiki/Ex-officio "Ex-officio") chairperson of the Youth Affairs Network of Queensland since 1997 (As of 2019[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit)). She has also served a member of a number of other bodies and organisations, including:[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)

* the Criminal Law Committee;
* [Law Council of Australia](/wiki/Law_Council_of_Australia "Law Council of Australia")
* Criminal Law Committee, [Queensland Law Society](/wiki/Queensland_Law_Society "Queensland Law Society")
* Equal Rights Alliance
* Australian Women Again Violence Alliance
* National Coronial Reform, [Federation of Community Legal Centres](/wiki/Community_legal_centre "Community legal centre")
* Criminal Justice Network

She has been appointed to state and national working groups on a range of legal and social issues, and has also contributed to international forums, such as meetings convened by the [UN Office on Drugs and Crime](/wiki/UN_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime "UN Office on Drugs and Crime") to develop draft UN Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-Custodial Measures for Women Offenders; sessions of the Commission on the Status of Women; and conferences on [crime prevention](/wiki/Crime_prevention "Crime prevention") and criminal justice.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)

In November 2016 Kilroy was appointed to Queensland's Sentencing Advisory Council.[[8]](#cite_note-8) She believes that the council has an important role to play in educating the public, to counteract the "law-and-order hysteria" seen in the media and spruiked by politicians.[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4)

In early 2019, she led a [crowd-funding](/wiki/Crowd-funding "Crowd-funding") campaign called #freeher to pay off the court debts of Indigenous women in [Western Australia](/wiki/Western_Australia "Western Australia") who had been imprisoned for defaulting on fines, raising over A$400,000 and enabling the release of 11 women.[[9]](#cite_note-ausstory-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) Amendments to the WA legislation were passed in 2020, partly as result of the recommendation from the coronial inquiry into the [death of Ms Dhu](/wiki/Death_of_Ms_Dhu "Death of Ms Dhu"), who [died in police custody](/wiki/Aboriginal_deaths_in_custody "Aboriginal deaths in custody").[[11]](#cite_note-11)

In April 2020 Kilroy contracted [COVID-19](/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") after travelling to the United States with her friend and colleague Boneeta-Marie Mabo, with both becoming so unwell that they were admitted to hospital.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Around 18 months of contracting the virus, in September 2021, she was still suffering from [Long COVID](/wiki/Long_COVID "Long COVID"), with a debilitating range of symptoms.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

As of 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit) she is principal of the law firm Kilroy & Callaghan, where she leads a team of five, and [CEO](/wiki/CEO "CEO") of Sisters Inside. She is passionate about encouraging former offenders, and in particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and [culturally diverse](/wiki/Multiculturalism_in_Australia#Terminology "Multiculturalism in Australia") women to become criminal lawyers.[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1)

Beliefs and advocacy
--------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Beliefs and advocacy")]

Kilroy's experience of imprisonment led to her belief that unnecessary trauma caused by the prison system, including [solitary confinement](/wiki/Solitary_confinement "Solitary confinement") as a punishment for [self-harm](/wiki/Self-harm "Self-harm"), leads to a greater likelihood of women re-offending and ending up back in prison.[[1]](#cite_note-costi-1) Influenced by people such as the US academic, activist and former prisoner [Angela Davis](/wiki/Angela_Davis "Angela Davis"), Kilroy believes that the prison system fails in its mission to punish and rehabilitate, with more than half of women released from prison returning to spend another stint there.[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She names two other former prisoners as heroes of hers: [Nelson Mandela](/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi")[[14]](#cite_note-14)

She has said that there is a need to break down "racism, misogyny and sexism within the legal frameworks", and that harsher sentences are not the answer.[[4]](#cite_note-robertson2017-4) She points out that "The vast majority of women prisoners are imprisoned for minor, non-violent crimes... [which] are often poverty-related", with around 40% being [onremand](/wiki/Remand_(detention) "Remand (detention)"), as yet untried for their alleged crimes. She says:[[6]](#cite_note-shedefined-6)

> Too often women are imprisoned on remand for failures of the state. Failure to provide adequate income support, to support women leaving violent homes, to provide essential housing and health services, and to address multigenerational harm arising from colonisation.

She engages in public debate and advocates for women on a range of issues, including violence, [homelessness](/wiki/Homelessness "Homelessness"), [racism](/wiki/Racism_in_Australia "Racism in Australia"), mental health, [substance abuse](/wiki/Substance_abuse "Substance abuse"), poverty, [child protection](/wiki/Child_protection "Child protection"), sexual assault, and failures in government systems. She aims to reduce the rate of criminalisation and imprisonment of women and children, in particular the over-representation of [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander](/wiki/Aboriginal_and_Torres_Strait_Islander "Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander") within the criminal justice system, and to women reduce the impact of mothers' imprisonment on their children.[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)

Recognition
-----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Debbie_Kilroy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recognition")]

* 2003: [Order of Australia Medal](/wiki/Order_of_Australia_Medal "Order of Australia Medal")[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2004: [Australian Human Rights Medal](/wiki/Australian_Human_Rights_Medal "Australian Human Rights Medal")[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Emergent Woman Lawyer of the Year[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2010: Peace Women Award[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2014: [Churchill Fellowship](/wiki/Churchill_Fellowship "Churchill Fellowship")[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2016: shortlisted Queensland nomination for [Australian of the Year](/wiki/Australian_of_the_Year "Australian of the Year")[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3)
* 2019: keynote speaker at the [Law Institute of Victoria](/wiki/Law_Institute_of_Victoria "Law Institute of Victoria")'s Women in Leadership lunch[[15]](#cite_note-15)
* 2019: [Voltaire Human Rights Award](/wiki/Voltaire_Human_Rights_Award "Voltaire Human Rights Award")[[16]](#cite_note-16)

---------------------

* *[Australian Story](/wiki/Australian_Story "Australian Story")* on [ABC Television](/wiki/ABC_Television_(Australia) "ABC Television (Australia)") (2004[[3]](#cite_note-womensreg-3) and 2019)[[9]](#cite_note-ausstory-9)
* *Kilroy was Here*, a biography by [Kristina Olsson](/wiki/Kristina_Olsson "Kristina Olsson") (2005)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

**Bräcke Municipality** ([Swedish](/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Bräcke kommun*) is a [municipality](/wiki/Municipalities_of_Sweden "Municipalities of Sweden") in [Jämtland County](/wiki/J%C3%A4mtland_County "Jämtland County") in northern [Sweden](/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"). Its [seat](/wiki/Administrative_centre "Administrative centre") is located in [Bräcke](/wiki/Br%C3%A4cke "Bräcke").

The present municipality was formed in 1974 when "old" Bräcke Municipality was amalgamated with Kälarne and Revsund. The three former municipalities had been created in 1952. The number of original entities (as of 1863) were six. Due to the declining population in the area further amalgamations have been proposed, but rejected.

**Jämtland** (Swedish: [[ˈjɛ̌mːtland]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish "Help:IPA/Swedish") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Sv-J%C3%A4mtland.ogg "File:Sv-Jämtland.ogg")) is a historical [province](/wiki/Provinces_of_Sweden "Provinces of Sweden") (*landskap*) in the centre of [Sweden](/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") in [northern Europe](/wiki/Northern_Europe "Northern Europe"). It borders [Härjedalen](/wiki/H%C3%A4rjedalen "Härjedalen") and [Medelpad](/wiki/Medelpad "Medelpad") to the south, [Ångermanland](/wiki/%C3%85ngermanland "Ångermanland") to the east, [Lapland](/wiki/Lapland,_Sweden "Lapland, Sweden") to the north and [Trøndelag](/wiki/Tr%C3%B8ndelag "Trøndelag") and [Norway](/wiki/Norway "Norway") to the west. Jämtland covers an area of 34,009 square kilometres, 8.3% of Sweden's total area and is the second largest province in Sweden. It has a population of 115,331,[[1]](#cite_note-population-1) the majority of whom live in *Storsjöbygden*, the area surrounding lake [Storsjön](/wiki/Storsj%C3%B6n "Storsjön"). [Östersund](/wiki/%C3%96stersund "Östersund") is Jämtland's only city and is the [24th most populous city in Sweden](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Sweden_by_population "List of cities in Sweden by population"). The historical province is one of the least densely populated.

Jämtland was originally an autonomous [republic](/wiki/Republic "Republic"),[[2]](#cite_note-republic-2) its own [nation](/wiki/Nation "Nation")[[2]](#cite_note-republic-2) with its own [law](/wiki/Law "Law"), [currency](/wiki/Currency "Currency")[[3]](#cite_note-3) and [parliament](/wiki/Parliament "Parliament"). Jämtland was conquered by [Norway](/wiki/Norway "Norway") in 1178 and stayed Norwegian for over 450 years until it was ceded to Sweden in 1645. The province has since been Swedish for roughly 370 years, though the population did not gain Swedish citizenship until 1699. The province's identity is manifested with the humorous culture and marketing concept of a [republic](/wiki/Republic_of_Jamtland "Republic of Jamtland") within the kingdom of Sweden, although this is only done semi-seriously.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Historically, socially and politically Jämtland has been a special territory between Norway and Sweden. This in itself is symbolized in the province's coat of arms where Jämtland, the silver moose, is threatened from the east and from the west. During the unrest period in Jämtland's history (1563–1677) it shifted alignment between the two states through occupations no less than 13 times.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Etymology
---------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6stenen.jpg/250px-Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6stenen.jpg)](/wiki/File:Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6stenen.jpg)

Frösö Runestone



Main article: [Etymology of Jämtland](/wiki/Etymology_of_J%C3%A4mtland "Etymology of Jämtland")

Jämtland's name derives from its inhabitants, the Jamts.[[6]](#cite_note-etymology-6) The name can be traced back to Europe's northernmost [runestone](/wiki/Runestone "Runestone"), the [Frösö Runestone](/wiki/Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6_Runestone "Frösö Runestone") from the 11th century, where it is found as *eotalont* (normalized [Old Norse](/wiki/Old_Norse "Old Norse"): *Jamtaland*). The [root](/wiki/Root_(linguistics) "Root (linguistics)") of Jamt ([Old West Norse](/wiki/Old_West_Norse "Old West Norse"): *jamti*), and thus Jämtland, derives from the [Proto-Germanic](/wiki/Proto-Germanic "Proto-Germanic") [word stem](/wiki/Word_stem "Word stem") *emat-* meaning persistent, efficient, enduring and hardworking.[[6]](#cite_note-etymology-6) The [Proto-Norse](/wiki/Proto-Norse "Proto-Norse") [prefix](/wiki/Prefix "Prefix") *eota* (*jamta*) is a [genitive](/wiki/Genitive "Genitive") [plural](/wiki/Plural "Plural") case.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Olav_den_helliges_saga_-_Torodd_Arnljott_Geline_-_H._Egedius_-_H._Egedius.jpg/250px-Olav_den_helliges_saga_-_Torodd_Arnljott_Geline_-_H._Egedius_-_H._Egedius.jpg)](/wiki/File:Olav_den_helliges_saga_-_Torodd_Arnljott_Geline_-_H._Egedius_-_H._Egedius.jpg)

Jämtland does not mean "the even country" but rather "Jamts' land". In this picture the [Viking](/wiki/Viking "Viking") Arnljot Gelline from Jämtland is seen moving through the landscape.

It is not known how the Jamts got their name. One possible explanation is presented in the [Icelandic](/wiki/Iceland "Iceland") work *[Heimskringla](/wiki/Heimskringla "Heimskringla")* from the 13th century. In the [Saga of Håkon Góði](/wiki/Heimskringla#Contents "Heimskringla"), [Snorri Sturluson](/wiki/Snorri_Sturluson "Snorri Sturluson") narrates about Kettil Jamti, a son of Anund [Jarl](/wiki/Jarl_(title) "Jarl (title)") from [Sparbu](/wiki/Sparbu "Sparbu") in Trøndelag who fled from Norway when [Harald Fairhair](/wiki/Harald_I_of_Norway "Harald I of Norway") united the country with brute force in the 9th century. His descendants then came to bear his [name](/wiki/Family_name "Family name").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] An alternative explanation comes from the excessive iron production that took place in the province before the [Viking Age](/wiki/Viking_Age "Viking Age"). A [folk etymological](/wiki/Folk_etymology "Folk etymology") theory is that the name ought to have something to do with the "even" (as in level or flat) parts around the [lake](/wiki/Lake "Lake") [Storsjön](/wiki/Storsj%C3%B6n "Storsjön"). This theory is based on the similarity between the Swedish words *jämt* (from *emat-*) and *jämnt* (from Germanic *\*ebna*, "even").[[6]](#cite_note-etymology-6)

The name Jämtland with an [Ä](/wiki/%C3%84 "Ä") is a 20th-century Swedish alteration of the older spelling *Jemtland*. Localities settled by Jamtish emigrants such as [Jemtland](/w/index.php?title=Jemtland,_Ringsaker&action=edit&redlink=1 "Jemtland, Ringsaker (page does not exist)") in [Ringsaker Municipality](/wiki/Ringsaker_Municipality "Ringsaker Municipality"), Norway and [Jemtland](/wiki/Jemtland,_Maine "Jemtland, Maine") in [Maine](/wiki/Maine "Maine"), United States were founded before the alteration occurred. In the nearby Norwegian province of Trøndelag old settlements such as [Jamtøya](/w/index.php?title=Jamt%C3%B8ya&action=edit&redlink=1 "Jamtøya (page does not exist)"), [Jamtgarden](/w/index.php?title=Jamtgarden&action=edit&redlink=1 "Jamtgarden (page does not exist)") and [Jamtåsen](/w/index.php?title=Jamt%C3%A5sen&action=edit&redlink=1 "Jamtåsen (page does not exist)") all use the prefix *Jamt-*, just like the regional name, however the [Trøndersk](/wiki/Tr%C3%B8ndersk "Trøndersk") name for Jämtland is *Jamtlainn*,[[7]](#cite_note-verdal-7) whilst the Jamtish name is *Jamtland*. As the d is silent the form *Jamtlann* is also common. The regional name *Jamtland* has only status as an official form in [Nynorsk](/wiki/Nynorsk "Nynorsk")[[7]](#cite_note-verdal-7) and [Icelandic](/wiki/Icelandic_language "Icelandic language"),[[8]](#cite_note-8) but is popularly used among locals which is one of the reasons as to why the regional museum was given the dialectal name [Jamtli](/wiki/Jamtli "Jamtli") (Swedish *jämtsk backsluttning*),[[9]](#cite_note-9) "Jamtish hillside".

Main article: [History of Jämtland](/wiki/History_of_J%C3%A4mtland "History of Jämtland")

### Prehistory

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=J%C3%A4mtland&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Prehistory")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Elanden_van_Glosa_20juli2005.jpg/330px-Elanden_van_Glosa_20juli2005.jpg)](/wiki/File:Elanden_van_Glosa_20juli2005.jpg)

Petroglyphs in [Glösa](/wiki/Gl%C3%B6sa "Glösa"), made approximately 5,000 years ago, displaying primarily moose. Several internal [organs](/wiki/Organ_(anatomy) "Organ (anatomy)") have been painted out. The carvings are very similar to the ones found in [Moelv](/w/index.php?title=Moelv_(Tr%C3%B8ndelag)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Moelv (Trøndelag) (page does not exist)") in Trøndelag and also resemble the [cave art](/wiki/Cave_art "Cave art") in [Altamira](/wiki/Cave_of_Altamira "Cave of Altamira"), [Spain](/wiki/Spain "Spain"). A carved ram from Glösa appears in [Krokom's](/wiki/Krokom_Municipality "Krokom Municipality") [coat of arms](/wiki/Coat_of_arms "Coat of arms").

Some finds from the time before humans have been discovered in Jämtland, most notably the remains from a [woolly mammoth](/wiki/Woolly_mammoth "Woolly mammoth") in [Pilgrimstad](/wiki/Pilgrimstad "Pilgrimstad").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The first humans came to Jämtland from the west across [the Keel](/wiki/Scandinavian_Mountains "Scandinavian Mountains") approximately 7000–6000 [BC](/wiki/Before_Christ "Before Christ"), after the [last ice age](/wiki/Last_glacial_period "Last glacial period").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] The climate was at the time much warmer than today and trees such as [oak](/wiki/Oak "Oak") were growing at the top of today's mountains. Several thousand archaeological remains have been located in the province, predominantly near old camp-sites, beaches and lakes. The oldest settlement found is located at [Foskvattnet](/w/index.php?title=Foskvattnet&action=edit&redlink=1 "Foskvattnet (page does not exist)"), not far way from the so-called [Fosna culture](/wiki/Fosna-Hensbacka_culture "Fosna-Hensbacka culture"), this settlement has been dated to 6600 BC. In Jämtland the moose was the dominant prey, which is clearly shown on [petroglyphs](/wiki/Petroglyph "Petroglyph") and rock paintings in for example [Gärde](/wiki/G%C3%A4rde "Gärde") and [Glösa](/wiki/Gl%C3%B6sa "Glösa"). Jämtland has over 20,000 documented [ancient monuments](/wiki/Ancient_monument "Ancient monument"), the oldest one being an arrowhead found in Åflo near [Kaxås](/wiki/Kax%C3%A5s "Kaxås") in [Offerdal](/wiki/Offerdal "Offerdal") parish possibly older than 8,000 years, which would make it one of the oldest Stone Age finds in all of Sweden.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Rock paintings found in Jämtland often collocates with various [trapping pits](/wiki/Trapping_pit "Trapping pit") and well over 10,000 pits used for hunting have been located, which is much more than any other Scandinavian region. Trapping or hunting pits were placed in areas in close proximity of the hunted animal in question, usually in known places where the animals moved. Because of this there are several places where pits have been dug separately in lines stretching on for miles throughout the landscape. Several [place names](/wiki/Place_name "Place name") in Jämtland still display the significance these pits had to the tribes.
